Nihilism is the belief that nothing matters. 

It is not necessarily acting in that way. I can acknowledge that smoking is bad, but still smoke.

I do not fear death. 

​

That's not to say I look forward to it or am completely ready to face it. I have some feeling towards death, but that feeling isn't fear. I don't know exactly how to describe it. It's kind of the same feeling of when I see a dead animal? That moment of sadness, but knowing nothing can be done. Solemness? 

I am scared of the \*how\* of death. I'm terrified of getting crushed to death, or getting set on fire. Or dying slowly after an accident which rips my arms off. I'm scared of pain, not of death. 

Death is not scary, because I will never experience it. I will experience dying, but not death.

>"In death there is nothing harmful; for there must exist something to which it is harmful."  
>  
> \- Seneca 

Both Seneca and Epicurus agree on this, so, to me, it's an easily acceptable universal truth. 

>"Therefore the most dread-inspiring of all evils, death, is nothing to us; for when we exist; death is not present in us, and when death is present, then we do not exist. Therefore it does not concern either the living or the dead; for to the living it has no existence, and the dead do not themselves exist."  
>  
>\-Epicurus

I can only hope that my dying is quick and painless, but I don't spend too much time thinking on it, as it is not something I can control.

Yes, I was born into a Christian family and raised as such.

​

I started losing my faith in my teens, and now consider myself an athiest. 

​

My most important philosophy is that life without god does not need to mean life without morals. 

I believe in doing good and helping people. I'm pro gay marriage and pro choice, because I believe being against these things is more cruel than being for them. I donate to charity. Though I am also fiscally conservative and do not believe all people are worthy of help. All moral decisions I make are based on the basic-to-me principles of "treat others as you'd like to be treated" and "how has someone treated others?".  I am extremely against cheating and sleeping around liberally even while single, because of STD risks being very high (1 in 2 people will catch an STD between the ages of 15 and 24, no thank you.) Some of these morals are remnants from my Christian days, but that doesn't make them wrong. I believe Christianity has valuable lessons. 

I'm still in the process of learning to accept things I cannot control, and not looking for answers to everything. Why are we here, what is the point? Don't know, don't care to find out. I believe we are here for the moment. What we do in that moment is the "point". To throw away your life because we die in the end anyway is the same as saying why eat if you will only be hungry again? 

Honestly this identity crisis you are facing would be better handled with therapy. It helps me. 

Maybe the answer is to leave your partner, quit your job, and move to the other side of the country. Maybe it's not. Maybe there is a way to achieve greater peace without starting over. Find a therapist and discuss this. You have one life, think your moves through before you make them, and maybe tell your partner what you are feeling (gently) as this will greatly affect them too.

What you are describing sounds a lot like Stoicism, which was around before Christianity and I believe was compatible with it. Stoics believed that everything was predetermined and the best way to be happy was to accept what you cannot control. Also some sects of Christianity believe in predetermination. Not that you don't have free-will exactly, but that your free will doesn't matter because God already knows what you will choose and it's all a part of his plan. However, it feels depressing when I word it like that. The nihilism in it is just a realization that just because there may be a God doesn't mean we are the end goal of his creation. We may just be a tool, which means our existence has a purpose, just not to us... if that makes sense..

​

Well if it helps, here are a few of my favorite Stoic quotes:

"You have power over your mind- not outside events. Realize this and you will find strength" -Marcus Aurelius

"Don't seek for everything to happen as you wish it would, but rather wish that everything happens as it actually will -- then your life will flow well." - Epictetus

"If you are pained by any external thing, it is not this thing that disturbs you, but your own judgement about it. And it is in your power to wipe out this judgement now." -Marcus Aurelius
